title: Anand against Carlsen, Chennai 2013, game 6: a pawn up that is not yet a win, and how Carlsen won anyway
outcomes: Tries key moments before seeing the move and compares the attempt with the engine's first choice
Names what a trade gives and costs before making it, and checks the ending that results (23...Bxe3, 39...Rxe3)
Counts the pawns at each stage (one up, two up, one up, level) and says why a pawn up in a rook ending is often not yet a win: the pieces' activity and a passed pawn decide it

steps.text: **Anand (White) against Carlsen (Black)**, game 6 of the 2013 world championship match, Chennai, 16 November 2013. Carlsen won in 67 moves. The opening was a Ruy Lopez with a slow d3, not a sharp line. You will watch a quiet position turn into a won rook ending, and decide eight moments yourself. Boards show only the few moves that matter. Engine numbers are ratings at depth 16, not proof [V].

steps.text: **What a quiet position looks like.** Neither side has a loose piece, a weak pawn or an open file to attack. When the engine reads a position as level, the player who wants more has to change something: the pawn structure, the piece placement or the number of pieces. Carlsen's game is a series of small changes of that kind, each rated close to level by the engine. [I]

steps.text: **A concession, and what it buys.** White's pawns on e3 and e4 are doubled: they stand on one file and cannot guard each other. In return, White's rooks get the half-open f-file, and Black has given up the bishop that had been aimed at f2. At depth 16 the engine reads the result as level, so the trade wins nothing yet; it only changes the structure. Before any trade, ask what it gives and what it costs.

steps.text: **Space and trades.** Black's pawn on c4 took room on the queenside, White's d4 opened the centre, and one pair of rooks went off. This is not yet one side converting an edge: the engine rates each checked position up to move 31 as level or slightly better for one side. A common idea says the side that is ahead should trade, since a smaller army has fewer ways to counterattack [I]. The counter-case: trades also remove your attackers. Ask what is left after the last recapture.

steps.text: **Trade into an ending you have checked.** Carlsen did not trade queens because trading is good in general. The line he chose leaves him a pawn up in a rook ending, and the line that keeps queens was rated about level. A trade pays when the position after the last recapture is better for you than the one you leave. Count what is left, then ask who has the more active pieces. [I]

steps.text: **A pawn given for activity.** The pawn offer on move 44 leaves Black two pawns up, five to three. White's rook is then free to go after b5, and the engine rates the position after the capture as level (depth 16, claim above). Why White offered it we cannot prove; our guess is that rook activity was worth more than the pawn. [H] Choose below.

steps.text: **A pawn up is not yet a win.** Count first. Move 41: Black has five pawns to four. After the pawn offer on move 44: five to three. After 49.Rxb5: four to three. After 59.Rxc4: three each. A pawn up in a rook ending is often drawn because the defender's rook is active. Here the count fell to level, yet Black kept the better pieces: king on e3, rook behind the pawns, White's rook tied to them. Count the pawns, then ask whose king and rook are more active. [I]

steps.text: **What the numbers say.** At depth 16 the engine reads the checked positions as level for long stretches: after the queen trade, around move 49 and at move 55. At that depth 55.Rf8 is at least a quarter-pawn below the best move, and 57.Rg8+ at least 0.3 pawns below it (claims above). So the win looks like a long squeeze of small slips, with Black's king and pawns gaining time while White's rook did not [I]. We checked only these moves, not every move.

**One plan for converting.** The last three decisions form a plan. First the king goes up to the pawns (58...Ke3). Then a pawn block stops White's rook attacking along the fourth rank (59...f4). Then a pawn break makes a passed pawn (60...h3, and the f-pawn runs). King up, rook free, passed pawn: ask which of the three is missing when you convert. [I]

steps.prompt: Write the one question you would ask before any trade. Then apply it to 23...Bxe3: what did the trade give, what did it cost, and what was left after the last recapture?

steps.text: **A model answer.** The question: what does this trade give me, what does it cost, and what does the position look like after the last recapture? Applied to 23...Bxe3: Black gave up the bishop aimed at f2 and got White's pawns doubled on e3 and e4, while White got the half-open f-file. The engine reads the result as level (depth 16), so the trade was fair, not a win. [I] Compare your own answer with this one.

**To remember.**
1. A level position changes only when someone changes the structure, the pieces or the trades.
2. Name what each trade gives and costs.
3. Trade only into an ending you have checked.
4. Count the pawns before you call a position better. A pawn up often needs activity, and usually a passed pawn, to win; the other side may win one back.
5. In rook endings, keep the rook active and bring the king forward.
6. Engine numbers are ratings at a depth, not proofs.
